A puffball is most commonly a type of fungus — a living organism similar to a mushroom — that grows in a perfectly round or ball-like shape, almost like a small white balloon sitting on the ground. The name tells you exactly what it does: when it is ripe and ready, you can give it a gentle squeeze or even just tap it, and it releases a sudden puff of powdery material into the air, like a tiny smoke bomb. That powdery cloud is actually millions of spores — the microscopic seeds that the puffball uses to reproduce and spread.

A young puffball looks like a smooth, firm, white ball. It has no visible cap, no gills underneath, and often no obvious stem — it's just a clean, round lump sitting on the soil, grass, or rotting wood. If you cut one open when it is young, the inside looks like a solid block of pure white, almost like a marshmallow or a block of tofu.

As it ages and matures, the inside slowly transforms. The white flesh turns yellow, then olive green, then dark brown and powdery. By the time it is fully mature, the entire inside is nothing but dry, dusty spores ready to be released. At this stage, even a raindrop, a passing animal, or a gust of wind is enough to make it "puff" and release its spores.

Puffballs come in a surprisingly wide range of sizes:

  • Some are tiny, barely bigger than a marble.
  • Others are the size of a golf ball or a tennis ball.
  • And then there is the giant puffball, which can grow as large as a basketball, a football, or even bigger — sometimes the size of a human head. These giants can weigh several kilograms and are hard to miss when you spot one in a field or a meadow.

Puffballs are found all over the world. They typically grow in open grassy areas like meadows, lawns, and fields, as well as in forests and woodlands near decaying wood and leaf matter. They tend to appear in late summer and autumn, though this can vary by region and species.

Yes — but only under the right conditions. Young puffballs that are pure white all the way through when cut open are considered edible and are even enjoyed as food in many cultures. They have a mild, earthy taste. People slice and fry them, much like tofu.

However, you must follow two critical rules before eating one:

  1. Cut it open and check that the inside is completely and uniformly white. If there is any yellow, olive, or brown coloring beginning inside, it is past its edible stage and should not be eaten.
  2. Confirm it is genuinely a puffball and not a young, still-enclosed poisonous mushroom (like the deadly Amanita species) that could look similar on the outside. This is why foragers always slice the specimen open — a true puffball will be solid white inside with no hidden shape or structure; a dangerous look-alike will reveal the outline of a developing cap and gills inside.

While the fungus is the primary meaning, the word is also used more loosely in everyday English in two additional ways:

1. Something soft, round, and fluffy. People sometimes call a small, round, fluffy animal — like a particularly chubby kitten, a baby bird, or a little dog with thick fur — a "puffball." It is a playful, affectionate term meaning the creature is so round and soft that it resembles a puffball mushroom.

2. A style of skirt in fashion. A puffball skirt (also called a bubble skirt) is a type of skirt designed to be gathered and tucked inward at the hem, creating a round, balloon-like, puffy silhouette. It puffs outward at the hips and narrows toward the bottom — making it look, quite literally, like a puffball. This style was very popular in the 1980s and has reappeared in fashion trends several times since.
The Single Best Way to Remember It

Think of the word in two parts: puff + ball.

  • Ball = it is perfectly round, like a ball.
  • Puff = it puffs out a cloud of powder when disturbed.

Every meaning of the word connects back to this image — something round and soft that either literally puffs (the fungus), looks puffed out (the skirt), or seems soft and round like a puffed-up ball (the fluffy animal).
